# Confidence Intervals

```{r}
library(tidyverse, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

## Proportion

Let the parameter $\pi$ denote a population proportion. We can estimate $\pi$
by producing a point estimate and an interval estimate. There are different
estimators that produce interval estimates for $\pi$.

```{r}
simulate_data <- function(theta, n, idx) {
  
  # Simulate data and estimate parameter
  X <- rbinom(n = 1, size = n, prob = theta)
  theta_hat <- X / n
  
  # Get results
  tibble(theta = theta, n = n, idx = idx, theta_hat = theta_hat)
  
}
```

First, we simulate data:

```{r}
# Ensure reproducibility
set.seed(3729)

# Define settings for simulation
N <- 100L

ns <- seq(5L, 100L, 5L)
thetas <- seq(0.01, 0.99, 0.01)

settings <- tibble(theta = thetas) |>
  crossing(n = ns) |>
  crossing(idx = 1L:N) |>
  arrange(theta, n, idx)

sim_dat <- pmap_dfr(.l = settings, .f = simulate_data, .progress = TRUE)
```

### Wald Interval

The Wald interval is calculated as follows:

$$
\hat{\pi} \pm z_{1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{\pi} (1 - \hat{\pi})}{n}}
$$

We calculate the Wald CI for the simulated data.

```{r}
# Calculate the Wald confidence intervals
wald_dat <- sim_dat |>
  mutate(
    ci_wald_ll = theta_hat - qnorm(p = 0.975)*sqrt((theta_hat*(1-theta_hat))/n),
    ci_wald_ul = theta_hat + qnorm(p = 0.975)*sqrt((theta_hat*(1-theta_hat))/n),
    ci_wald_cov = between(theta, ci_wald_ll, ci_wald_ul)
  )

# Calculate the Wald CI coverage
wald_smr <- wald_dat |>
  group_by(theta, n) |>
  summarise(ci_wald_cov = mean(ci_wald_cov), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r}
# Ensure reproducibility
set.seed(3729)

# Define settings for simulation
N <- 100L

ns <- seq(5L, 100L, 5L)
thetas <- seq(0.01, 0.99, 0.01)

settings <- tibble(theta = thetas) |>
  crossing(n = ns) |>
  crossing(idx = 1L:N) |>
  arrange(theta, n, idx)

sim_dat <- pmap_dfr(.l = settings, .f = simulate_data, .progress = TRUE)
```

```{r}
ggplot(wald_smr, aes(x = n, y = ci_wald_cov, color = theta, group = theta)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = "y ~ x") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, color = "darkred") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "Sample size", y = "CI Wald: Coverage") +
  scale_color_gradient2(low = "yellow", high = "red")
```

The following figure shows the coverage at different sample sizes when sampling
from three different populations with the parameters $\theta_1 = 0.01$, $\theta_2
= 0.50$, and $\theta_3 = 0.99$.

An increase in sample size results in a better coverage. The coverage at the
extremes of the parameter space is lower compared to other areas of the parameter
space.

```{r}
wald_smr |>
  filter(theta %in% c(0.01, 0.50, 0.99)) |>
  mutate(theta = as_factor(theta)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = ci_wald_cov, color = theta)) +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess", formula = "y ~ x") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, color = "darkred") +
    theme_classic() +
    labs(title = "Coverage for Wald CI") +
    labs(x = "Sample size", y = "Coverage", color = "Theta")
```

### Wilson Interval

The Wilson interval is calculated as follows:

$$
\frac
  {\hat{\pi} + \frac{z^2_{1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}}}{2n}}
  {1 + \frac{z^2_{1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}}}{n}}
  \pm \frac
    {z_{1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p} \hat{q}}{n} + \frac{z^2_{1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}}}{4n^2}}}
    {1 + \frac{z^2_{1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}}}{n}}
$$
